messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Chanthon Meas is a 68-year-old widowed Cambodian American man who has spent the better part of four decades working as a public defender in a mid-sized city in California. He is a careful, deliberate man — colleagues describe him as measured in court, patient with clients others have given up on — and it is precisely that carefulness that makes what happened to his son all the more unbearable to him. Eleven months ago, Chanthon's youngest son, Dara, was beaten severely outside a convenience store by a group of men who had followed him from a nearby bar. Dara survived, but sustained a traumatic brain injury that left him with permanent cognitive impairment and partial paralysis on his left side. Chanthon arrived at the hospital to find Dara unconscious, and what he heard in those first moments — the flat, mechanical rhythm of the ventilator, a nurse's voice calling a code, the sound of his own name being said by a doctor whose expression told him everything before the words did — has never fully left him.

In the weeks that followed, Chanthon found that his memories of that night did not arrange themselves into anything coherent. He could not hold the sequence of events in order; instead, fragments surfaced without warning and without context — the fluorescent glare of the hospital corridor, the specific timbre of the ventilator, a half-heard conversation between nurses that he could not reconstruct but could not stop hearing. When these pieces came, they brought with them a grief so total that he could not speak, could not move, could only sit with it until it passed. He had come to believe that there was something wrong with the way his mind was working, that the fractured quality of his memory meant he had failed even to properly witness what had happened to his son.

He began checking the locks on his apartment door each night before bed — first once, then three times, then more. He had come to understand, in a way that felt entirely rational to him, that dangerous people were everywhere and that he had simply not been paying sufficient attention before. At work, this translated into a new and exhausting alertness. The public defender's office requires him to meet regularly with clients who have been charged with violent offences, and Chanthon now found himself scanning each face for signs of threat, reading posture and eye contact with an intensity that left him depleted by midday. He had begun requesting that a colleague sit in on certain client meetings, offering procedural justifications that his supervisor accepted without question, though Chanthon himself knew the real reason. He was certain that he could no longer trust his own read of a room, and equally certain that the room might at any moment become dangerous.

He stopped watching television almost entirely. A crime drama, a news segment, even a documentary that drifted toward violence — any of these could land him somewhere he did not want to be. He had begun eating more in the evenings, working through whatever was in the kitchen after visiting Dara at the rehabilitation facility, and he understood this as something he was doing to get through the hours, though it brought him no real comfort. What frightened him most, sitting alone in his apartment, was not any single image but the sound — the ventilator, the nurse's voice — returning without invitation, insisting on being heard.

What finally brought Chanthon to seek help was a conversation with Dara's occupational therapist, who gently observed that Chanthon himself seemed to be struggling and asked whether he had anyone to talk to. He had not. His wife had died six years earlier, and he had managed that loss through work and routine, neither of which was holding him now. He came to his first appointment quiet and formal, uncertain what he was asking for. What he said, when asked what he hoped for, was simple: he wanted to be able to remember that night without it breaking him open every time, and he wanted to be present enough, clear enough, to be useful to Dara for whatever came next.
